item.title: What 'Healthy' Food Labels Leave Out
item.description:
Diet

What 'Healthy' Food Labels Leave Out

Health claims on packaged food often often don’t reflect overall nutrition.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • A study of 150,000 new food and beverage products found health claims are inconsistent signals of nutrition.
  • Some claims come with trade-offs, such as more sugar in “low-sodium” beverages.
  • Shoppers can treat front-of-package claims as a hint and use the Nutrition Facts panel for the full picture.
Source: Sia / Adobe Stock

These days, many food packages make a promise of nutrition: reduced fat, high fiber, whole grain, or non-GMO, to name a few. At first glance, these claims seem designed to help shoppers choose healthier options at the grocery store. But new Cornell research suggests they are a less reliable guide for better nutrition than many people assume.

In a new analysis published in Nature Food, Cornell food marketing researchers Pei Zhou, Miguel Gómez, and Harry Kaiser examined nearly 150,000 packaged food and beverage products launched in the United States between 2015 and 2024. Yuqing Zheng, an agricultural economist at the University of Kentucky, also contributed to the study.

4 Types of Food Package Claims

The research team grouped printed claims into four categories:

  • Minus: promises reduced levels of nutrients we should limit, such as lower sodium
  • Plus: promises added or increased beneficial nutrients, such as more fiber
  • Natural: indicates the food's production characteristics or ingredient origins are organic, non-GMO, or have no artificial additives
  • Functional: emphasizes physiological or health benefits, such as immune support.

To judge the overall nutrition of the product, the team used the U.K. Nutrient Profiling Model, a scoring system developed in Britain to regulate food marketing. Unlike a single-nutrient claim, the system weighs a product's entire profile: calories, sugar, sodium, saturated fat, fiber, protein, and fruit, vegetable, and nut content.

The researchers found more than half of new products included claims on their packages. Yet, about two-thirds of these products were classified as "less healthy" overall, according to the British nutrition model.

Products with some types of on-package claims tended to have slightly better overall nutrition than similar products without those claims, but this pattern was not consistent across all claim categories. Even when products with claims scored better, many were still considered less healthy overall. A claim highlighting one positive feature could also come with less favorable levels of other nutrients. For example, beverages claiming "low/no/reduced sodium" and "low/no/reduced saturated fat" had higher amounts of sugar. In dairy and eggs, as well as in meals and side dishes, "low/no/reduced trans fat" claims were associated with lower protein and higher saturated fat and sodium levels.

Even when a claim did match up with a better overall nutrition score, many of those products still landed in the "less healthy" category of the nutrient profiling system.

“Natural” Claims

"Natural" claims were the most common type, and it’s important to note that they do not necessarily convey information about nutrition quality, including levels of sugar, sodium, or fat, the study found. In the analysis, natural claims such as "no artificial flavors" or "no preservatives" were associated with poorer nutrition profiles in several food and beverage categories.

This is important because previous research shows that shoppers often read them as signs of healthfulness, a bias known as the halo effect.

The authors offer two explanations. First, food manufacturers could possibly make formulation trade-offs, where cutting one ingredient is offset by adding more of another. Second, food manufacturers may use selective signaling, in which a claim highlights one improvement while other nutritional qualities are not mentioned.

Shoppers pay attention to these claims, but they may not fully trust them. Those are the findings from a 2025 white paper published by the National Science Foundation. The paper found 83 percent of consumers report reading food labels before buying a product, and 78 percent said they prioritize health claims when doing so. But only 16 percent of survey participants considered such package nutrition claims as highly trustworthy, and 20 percent reported difficulty interpreting nutritional information.

The Cornell study does not suggest that companies are breaking the law. Nutritional claims are regulated for accuracy about the specific attribute they name, not for representing a product's entire nutritional profile. The authors also note the study’s limits: It is observational, covers newly launched products rather than what people actually buy, and did not measure how consumers respond to claims.

Nevertheless, federal regulators are rethinking food labels. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration updated its definition of "healthy" in 2024 and has proposed a new, front-of-package system that summarizes nutrition at a glance. Other countries have adopted different approaches to simplified front-of-package labeling, resembling similar systems in the United Kingdom, Mexico, and Chile

The take-home message: Claims on the front of food packages do not tell the full story. It’s important to check the back label for added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat. And when a label touts less of one thing, compare it with the regular version to see what the tradeoff was.

item.title: When Gender Bias Limits Safety for Survivors of IPV
item.description:
Domestic Violence

When Gender Bias Limits Safety for Survivors of IPV

Biases over who is a victim and who is a perpetrator can limit protections.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • LGBTQ+ survivors may face additional barriers when seeking help for intimate partner violence.
  • Biases over who is expected to be a victim and perpetrator can limit support for survivors.
  • Being believed and understood can be critical when someone reaches out for help.

I was standing over the hot stove. A filet of swordfish was crackling in the skillet. The smell of crispy-fried skin filled the kitchen. At the time, all I was thinking about was dinner.

Then, a loud bang nearly knocked me off my feet. “Open this damn door!” her voice shrieked from across the apartment, but I already knew who it was. She was back.

Source: Image by laughingfire from Pixabay

In my panic, I somehow managed to shut off the burner without falling into a pan of scalding hot oil and fish. Then, I navigated my way at top speed through the kitchen and into the living room, dodging furniture, rugs, and the cat - probably looking like an athlete through an obstacle course.

The banging continued; it grew louder. By the time I was at the door, her demands for me to open it were turning into threats. “Open this door, or you'll see what happens!" The wooden frame shuddered with each blow from her fist. My heart pounded along with it. I thanked my earlier self for having the foresight to install a deadbolt, though I never expected it to be so useful.

With trembling hands, I grabbed my cell phone. My fingers could barely dial. My mind had to stop and remember the numbers 9-1-1. At that moment, even basic things seemed like quantum physics. I also ignored the 'emergency call' option on my locked home screen. You know, the annoying one you have to swipe away because you didn't mean to pull it up? Because you're never actually in an emergency… until you are. It didn't even occur to me to use it. Instead, my shaking fingers fumbled through the options to unlock my phone, opening the touchpad and dialing the numbers 9-1-1. It was like one of those nightmares where you have to run, but your legs move in slow motion. Everything I did felt like it was taking an eternity.

My mind was racing. Someone on the other line was asking me questions, way too many questions. The banging echoed against the walls. My chest was tight. The wooden door was cracking under pressure. “It’s my ex,” I breathed into the phone, “She’s trying to break down my door! Send help.”

But rather than immediately send help, the dispatcher on the other line was confused whenever I used female pronouns. They kept hesitating, asking for more information. Meanwhile, the door kept cracking. Their hesitation was a move that could have cost me my life.

Biases About Who Can Be a Perpetrator Can Limit Safety

While LGBTQ acceptance becomes more widespread and victims from this community have begun to feel more comfortable reaching out for help to escape intimate partner abuse, progress is slow. Recent laws aim to protect partners from intimate violence without regard to gender or sexuality, but negative biases can still corrupt an individual’s perspective. Sometimes, those individuals are the ones in a position to end an abusive situation, and their biases can be deadly.

Members of the LGBTQ community face a situation many marginalized groups face today called minority stress. This added burden comes from various stressors linked to being part of an underrepresented or stigmatized minority. The lack of protection from laws and unequal allocation of resources leaves them less protected in society simply because of who they are. It attacks their very identity. These concerns can create a painful dilemma: I need help, but what happens if the people I turn to don't understand my situation?

That concern isn't necessarily unfounded. Research has documented that LGBTQ+ survivors can encounter stigma and barriers when accessing domestic violence services, including concerns about discrimination, lack of LGBTQ+-specific resources, and providers who may not understand the dynamics of their relationships1.

All Survivors Need Support Regardless of Gender and Sexuality

LGBTQ+ survivors deserve responses that recognize their relationships without requiring them to explain or defend their identities first. And professionals don't have to know everything about every LGBTQ+ experience to provide a compassionate, appropriate response. They simply need to start with the same place they would start with anyone else: Assess the danger. Listen without assumptions. And help the person get safe.

Excerpted, in part, from my book Invisible Bruises: How a Better Understanding of the Patterns of Domestic Violence Can Help Survivors Navigate the Legal System.

If you are experiencing domestic violence or abuse, or are concerned about your safety after leaving a relationship, support is available. Call 800-799-SAFE (7233), or visit thehotline.org. Find a therapist in the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Secret to Maintaining Happiness as You Age
item.description:
Aging

The Secret to Maintaining Happiness as You Age

Preserving contentment through perceived control.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • The perception of control counteracts the negative effects of age-related changes.
  • Interventions to improve developmental adaptation over time improve perceptions of aging.
  • Perceiving loss can decrease happiness by undermining one’s concept of self.

“Young people don’t realize how good they have it,” we remark as adults. Young life flourishes with defining moments, age-related milestones, and motivation for the future. Mid-life experiences, in contrast, range from perceived crises to the wisdom of maturity, often both. Yet aging does not need to be a negative experience, particularly for people who are able to maintain a sense of peace and happiness throughout the lifespan through a perception of control. Research explains.

Source: Arek Socha / Pixabay

Age Is Just a Number: the Comfort of Control

As we age, change happens. The key to preserving peace and contentment may have less to do with the changes, whether positive or negative, and more to do with perceived control over changing circumstances.

Maria Wirth et al. (2026) examined how perception of control impacts individual awareness of age-related change and happiness.[i] They begin by acknowledging that in late adulthood, an awareness of age-related losses and the absence of age-related gains is associated with decreased feelings of well-being, including lower amounts of happiness. Yet the perception of control is a promising method of counteracting the negative effects of perceived age-related changes. In their research, studying 268 middle-aged and older adults ranging in age from 50 to 91, they found that perceptions of age-related losses were linked with lower levels of happiness only for participants who experienced a low level of perceived control. Wirth et al. thus recognize the importance of the perception of control on maintaining happiness in the face of age-related changes, and that interventions designed to improve developmental adaptation in later years should include improved self-perceptions of aging and a stronger sense of control.

Realistic Recognition of Loss

As we age, we confront and accept changes in a variety of areas—physically, mentally, and financially, to name a few. Yet the awareness of age-related losses, whether we accept them or not, can impact personal happiness. Wirth et al. note, for example, that merely accommodating something as basic as changes in physical fitness might include limiting physical activity to avoid injury, which could lead to additional loss of existing physical capability. More broadly, avoiding or limiting pleasurable activities or behaviors can negatively impact enjoyment of life, which is a basic contributor to happiness.

Wirth et al. recognize that the perception of loss may decrease feelings of happiness by undermining one’s concept of self. Perceiving gains, on the other hand, should improve happiness and can enhance strivings for resource accumulation, improve the appreciation of social life and relationships, enhance life experiences, and spark desire to engage in pleasant activities. Conversely, a perceived absence of age-related gains can cause individual happiness to decrease.

Controlling the Narrative Cultivates Contentment

Wirth et al. recognize that maintaining or improving quality of life strongly relies on individual perception of control—the extent to which actions can bring results. Perceiving oneself as at the mercy of external factors could exacerbate the perception of age-related loss, while perceiving a high level of control could act as a motivational response that can spark active coping and adapting to age-related challenges. They note that perceiving a high level of control can even counteract negative stereotypes that are linked to perceived age-related losses.

Growing older involves gaining life experience and appreciation, acquiring wisdom and maturity in the process. Considering the fact that everyday happiness later in life is linked to daily changes in self-observations of aging and perceived control, there is cause to consider the positive aspects of aging. Credibility, experience, wisdom, patience, and other benefits of a life well-lived are personally fulfilling, are interpersonally engaging, and contribute to health, happiness, and peace.

item.title: Grey Is Fabulous, Just Not That Radical
item.description:
Beauty

Grey Is Fabulous, Just Not That Radical

Is embracing grey hair really a challenge to the beauty ideal?

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Grey hair's acceptance can save time and money without challenging dominant beauty standards.
  • The global beauty ideal prioritizes thinness, firmness, smoothness, and youth—not hair colour.
  • Grey-haired celebrities often meet other beauty norms, reinforcing rather than disrupting the ideal.
Helen Mirren
Source: Martin Kraft, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Coauthored by Heather Widdows and Jessica Sutherland, University of Warwick

The hair colour dominating 2026 is not blond, or brunette, or even "ginger spice" or "cherry cola," but grey, or if you prefer, silver. Last week, Good Housekeeping declared that “grey hair is the biggest beauty statement of the year.” It shows pictures of 10 celebrities who have embraced the grey: Glenn Close, Salma Hayek, Pru Leith, Andie MacDowell, Melinda Messenger, Helen Mirren, Sarah Jessica Parker, Sharon Stone, and Kristen Scott Thomas. The enthusiasm over Oliva Coleman’s transformation from her trademark short dark curls to long and flowing grey curls is gushing all over media and social media.

Grey can be a few strands as highlights, blended and woven with blonde or brown, creating a "natural ombre" or a luminous single colour. But in whatever form, grey is the hair colour of the moment.

Women & Home says "going grey is the most stylish thing you can do in 2026," also listing celebrities who have grey hair. Helen Mirren and Andie MacDowell feature on this list, too, along with others. Harper's Bazaar has an article this month on "9 ways to style long grey hair for autumn," with pictures of… have a guess? Yes, it's Andie and Helen again, and Sarah Jessica Parker in this one, too. Elle also has an article this month on the trend for going grey. This one is a "how-to" piece: "Arctic Blonde Is the ‘Grey Blending’ Colour Technique for Embracing Silver." No Andie or Helen here, presumably because they have already gone full grey and are not transitioning. Instead, the article is accompanied by pictures of Jerry Hall’s long locks, fresh from Celebrity Traitors.

Going Grey Does Not Challenge the Beauty Ideal

What should we take from this? Fabulous; we can now have grey hair. Hurrah. We can save time and money. At between £50 and £100 every six weeks for hair dye, this soon piles up. We are totally in with this trend. Full disclosure, one of us has gone from blond to grey over the last year or two (no prizes for guessing which of us!). It is great that grey hair is no longer taboo, and long grey hair, too. Even curls are being embraced—something close to our hearts as curly girls. So grey—hurrah!—but it is only hair. And changing hair colour does not challenge the beauty ideal.

The global beauty ideal focuses on the body and the face, not hair colour. Back in 2018, when Perfect Me was published, it was already the case that diversity in hair colour, eye colour, or skin colour did nothing to challenge the beauty ideal. The features of the global beauty ideal are thinness, firmness, smoothness, and youth. Since the pandemic, firmness and smoothness of the face and body have become even more demanding, as hard to believe as that is. When it comes to the beauty ideal, all types of hair colour are acceptable; they were in 2018, and they are now. In 2016, Vogue ran an article on grey hair being sexy, and in 2018, another on an editor embracing "the rebelliousness of silver hair." If more women feel less pressure to spend time and money on their hair that they don’t want to, that is fabulous. If they do want to keep their hair blonde, red, blue, or any other colour, they should of course keep dyeing it. We should not focus on practices, on what women do or don’t do to their bodies. Instead, we need to focus on the increasingly dominant global ideal, which requires more and more of us to take knives and needles to our faces and bodies, just to be normal.

Why Grey Hair on Otherwise Conforming Bodies Reinforces the Beauty Ideal

Hang on, you might say; isn’t this too quick? Grey hair is different from other hair colours. Grey hair is old hair. To go grey is to actively embrace being old, and therefore is, after all, challenging the ideal. But is it? As we’ve shown time and time again, challenging one feature of the beauty ideal does not challenge the ideal but reinforces it. This is true of body-positive campaigns, which challenge thinness, but otherwise promote firm, smooth, and glamourous bodies (often in pinup poses), or campaigns to grow body hair on thin, firm, and young bodies. The grey hair we are being sold is on otherwise conforming and beautiful people. If the grey we are permitted is the grey of Andie MacDowell and Helen Mirren, thin, glamourous, and beautifully made up, then the ideal remains dominant.

item.title: Changing Individual Behavior for Collective Well-Being
item.description:
Environment

Changing Individual Behavior for Collective Well-Being

An interview with Leaf Van Boven on collective well-being and addressing climate change.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Pro-social behavior is required for collective welfare and collective action.
  • People want to be pro-social; they just need the occasional reminder.
  • Climate change is, perhaps, the most challenging collective action problem of our time.
Source: Markus Spiske / Unsplash

When we, as individuals, encounter situations where we will be made worse off than others, we perceive relative deprivation. And yet, in many such situations, individuals are willing to sacrifice for collective well-being. This is a particularly relevant phenomenon when discussing macroeconomic challenges, such as climate change and public health. How do individuals decide when collective well-being is more important than their perceived relative deprivation? And how can communities organize with the understanding of the limitations of individual willingness to sacrifice?

What would it look like to minimize perceived relative deprivation and maximize collective well-being in the context of addressing climate change? To explore this question, I reached out to Leaf Van Boven, a researcher and professor at the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the director of the Environment, Decision, Judgment, and Identity Lab (EDJI) and has been investigating how cognitive, emotional, and social dynamics influence attitudes toward pressing issues like climate change. I asked Van Boven what I think are the five most important questions to help us understand how communities and individuals can approach maximizing collective well-being while minimizing perceived sacrifices of individuals.

JP: How do social preference and pro-social behavior impact personal and collective well-being?

LVB: Prosocial behavior is required for collective welfare and collective action. It’s a fundamental dilemma for humans: Maximizing personal and collective well-being requires some measure of self-sacrifice and pro-social behavior. Fortunately, there is ample research showing that people experience positive emotions and boosts in happiness when they behave pro-socially. So, what is good for society is good for us personally.

JP: How can individuals reshape their thinking to maintain their individual well-being while promoting collective well-being?

LVB: The reshaping is often a question of attention and awareness. Most people recognize the value of pro-social behavior—but they sometimes forget or become highly self-focused. In many cases, "reshaping" can be accomplished simply by reminding people of their personal prosocial values. People want to be pro-social; they just need the occasional reminder.

JP: How can we apply behavior science to climate change mitigation and adaptation?

LVB: Climate change is, perhaps, the most challenging collective action problem of our time. There are many views on the role of behavioral science in addressing it. My view is that, first and foremost, we need large-scale policy changes to support an energy transition away from fossil fuels and other carbon-intensive practices. It’s nearly impossible to “bend the curve” on climate change without policy change. In a sense, this simplifies the answer because the same insights behavioral science offers for other collective action problems—from civil rights to education to healthcare—apply equally, if not more so, to climate change. Civic action. Voting for policymakers who support climate policy. Activism to support climate policy. These are all critical parts of advancing climate policy. Of course, individual behavior change is good. But it needs to be in concert with broader systems change.

JP: How do we measure changes in pro-social behavior and associated impacts on collective well-being?

LVB: Behavioral science has a large toolbox for measuring pro-social behavior. This includes simple behavioral economic games, self-report measures of happiness and behavior, and incidental measures like facial expressions. There are many approaches to measuring prosocial behavior and well-being, and we should use all of them.

JP: How do we continue to iterate on and advance this work to develop more effective strategies to change behavior and improve collective well-being?

LVB: I’ll state the obvious. Iterating and advancing this work requires large-scale support for basic psychological science. The scientific endeavor, as a self-correcting, if imperfect, form of knowledge generation, is well equipped to make progress on critical questions about collective well-being. Scientists are eager to do that work. That requires a supporting infrastructure like that which has existed at the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health. Society and the policymakers we elect will have to decide if that work is worth continued investment.

item.title: How to Speak Up for Yourself
item.description:
Boundaries

How to Speak Up for Yourself

A simple 3-step technique to set boundaries.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Speaking up and advocating for yourself is an effective way to set boundaries.
  • Asking with curiosity can help start the conversations about issues that need to be addressed.
  • Listening with intent can help you collect the necessary information to advocate for yourself.
Source: Mina Rad / Unsplash

We live in a fast-paced society with competing work, family, and social responsibilities. Trying to keep up with everything is impossible. You have to pick and choose how you allocate your precious time and energy.

Setting boundaries is an essential skill for navigating life's frantic pace. If you do not cultivate this skill, life will spiral out of control.

There is a misconception that boundary setting is synonymous with saying "no." The truth is, boundary setting can take on a variety of forms. For example, asking for help or delegating tasks is an example of boundary setting. The same holds true for speaking up and advocating for yourself when you perceive some form of mistreatment or discrepancy in workload distribution.

Speaking up and advocating for yourself can feel prohibitive due to underlying emotional forces. These include feelings of guilt, shame, or obligation; being a people-pleaser; avoiding conflict; and having a fear of repercussions. I previously wrote a post about the emotional barriers to setting boundaries on Psychology Today.

However, another reason that people do not speak up for themselves is that they do not know how to. They lack a blueprint that can serve as a compass to effectively communicate their perspective.

If you find yourself in this situation, don't despair. Here is a simple, three-step technique to help you speak up and advocate for yourself.

1. Ask with curiosity

Let's create a hypothetical scenario. Imagine a situation in which your boss has assigned more work to you compared to your colleagues. Perhaps you have been assigned more shifts or projects than your peers.

Feeling frustrated with such a situation is completely valid. Your feelings are a signal to take action and bring the discrepancy to your boss's attention. Not speaking up and stewing in silence will not solve your predicament. Your silence only teaches your boss that it does not bother you to be assigned more work than your peers.

In this scenario, you ideally want to approach your boss at a time when they are available to discuss the matter. The setting of the conversation is important. Catching them off guard lowers your odds of achieving your desired outcome. It would be prudent to email them in advance that you would like 5-10 minutes of their time to discuss a work-related matter.

At the time of the meeting, you want to approach them with a curiosity mindset. You do not want to be confrontational or jump to any premature conclusions. Perhaps your boss did not notice the discrepancy and made an honest mistake. Another possibility is that they are short-staffed and assumed you would be OK with carrying the workload. After all, you are a hard-working, conscientious individual who always goes the extra mile. Is it not reasonable for them to assume that you would be OK with a few extra call shifts this month?

Regardless of their reasoning, you need to approach your boss to address the situation. A good starting point is to share your observation about the workload discrepancy and ask them about it with a curious tone.

An example can be:

"I noticed that I have six call shifts this month, but my colleagues only have three call shifts. Can you help me understand the discrepancy in workload?"

2. Listen with intent

Once they start explaining their reasoning, listen with intent. Let go of any preconceived notions and seek to fully understand their perspective.

Carefully listening to their explanation is critical because it will provide you with the necessary information to make an effective pitch and advocate for yourself.

3. Make your pitch

Once you have received the necessary information from their explanation, it is time to make your pitch. When making your pitch, you want to be assertive, but not aggressive. An aggressive tone is more likely to be met with resistance.

You also want to demonstrate that you emotionally understand your boss's predicament. This will increase the odds that they will work with you.

Finally, you want to offer potential solutions to the predicament. Proactively offering solutions increases your odds of gaining something valuable from the conversation. This is because you are directly impacted by the current predicament and more likely to come up with effective solutions than someone who is not directly impacted.

Here is an example of a pitch:

"Thank you for explaining the situation. I understand that you are in a difficult predicament because we are short-staffed and I appreciate you counting on me to get the job done. However, I cannot continue to take extra calls at this unsustainable pace. I wonder if next month, I can go back to my regular workload by distributing the calls more evenly among everyone in the department."

If the extra work does not bother you or your ask is met with resistance, then you can pivot to a different solution such as an increase in compensation or a promotion. Think of it as a win-win situation in which you help your boss fill the call shifts, and you gain something for going the extra mile.

When preparing your pitch, think of speaking up as an opportunity for personal and professional growth. Personal growth stems from refining your ability to speak up and advocate for yourself. Professional growth comes from making your pitch and gaining something in return.

Being equipped with a simple technique along with the necessary mindset can make it easier to speak up and advocate for yourself. Do not let this opportunity go to waste.

item.title: How to Listen to Other People
item.description:
Relationships

How to Listen to Other People

5 ways of listening that could change what's possible in your next conversation.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Empathic listening explores how someone feels, not what happened.
  • Generative listening can help two people discover an insight neither brought to the conversation.
  • Good listening means adapting to what a conversation needs, not always aiming for deeper discussion.

Think of the best conversations you've ever had—the ones that left you:

  • feeling closer to someone,
  • seeing something differently, or
  • thinking about something you'd never considered before.

Now think of all the conversations that feel like a waste of time.

What Makes the Difference?

We often think the difference comes down to who we're speaking to, or what we're talking about. But there's another factor we rarely consider, even though it creates what’s possible for the conversation:

How we listen.

Most of us think of listening as a single activity. But there are different ways to listen, each offering something different. And becoming aware of them might be the key to having more of the conversations we value.

1. Listening to Respond

Imagine a friend tells you they've just lost their job.

Before they've finished explaining what happened, you've already thought of a similar experience you want to share, some advice you could offer, or what you'd have done differently in their situation.

Of course, conversations require responses. There's nothing inherently wrong with wanting to contribute. But there's a difference between waiting for our turn to speak and allowing what someone says to shape what we contribute.

The problem arises when our eagerness to respond gets in the way of our opportunity to understand.

2. Listening to Know

For your friend who’s lost their job, rather than immediately offering advice, you might ask what happened, whether they saw it coming, or what they're planning to do next.

You're curious. You're asking questions. You're gathering information that you didn't have before.

But what if your friend isn’t ready to figure it all out, and simply wants to feel understood?

3. Listening to Empathise

Your friend explains that losing their job has shaken their confidence. They're worried about money, embarrassed to tell their family, or struggling with the loss of a role that gave them a sense of purpose.

Now, understanding what happened is less important than understanding how they're experiencing it.

Rather than immediately seeking more information or offering solutions, you might instead focus on simply making them feel understood.

In their work on active listening, psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson emphasised that listening well requires more than techniques—it requires genuine respect for the person speaking and a willingness to understand their perspective.1

Ways of responding when listening to empathise
Source: Dr Manu Sidhu / Made with ChatGPT

This creates the shift from “What can I discover from this person?” to “What is it like to be this person?”

4. Listening to Learn

As the conversation continues, your friend reflects on how much of their identity had become tied to their career. Perhaps they explain that losing their job has made them question what success really means to them. And something they say makes you reconsider your own relationship with work, ambition, or fulfilment.

Rather than simply trying to understand their experience, you're allowing their perspective to influence your own. This requires something more than curiosity—it requires:

Intellectual humility: the willingness to acknowledge that someone else might understand something we don't, and the openness to reconsider what we already believe.

But beyond learning something from each other, what if your conversation surfaces new insights that neither of you had before?

5. Listening to Discover

Your friend admits that although they're worried about finding another job, they weren't actually happy in their previous job.

You share something you read on the difference between being good at something and finding it fulfilling. They build on it, explaining that financial security matters to them, but status matters less than they once thought.

Then, a new possibility emerges: their next job doesn't need to satisfy every ambition. They could pursue financial stability while finding other ways to cultivate the parts of themselves that their career had neglected.

MIT Researcher Otto Scharmer calls this generative listening, the deepest of his Four Levels of Listening, in which openness and attention create space for new insights to emerge.2

This might explain why some conversations feel so extraordinary. We leave with more than information, understanding, or even a changed perspective. We leave with an insight that didn't exist for either of us when the conversation began.

The 5 Ways of Listening
Source: Dr Manu Sidhu / Made with ChatGPT

Bonus—Listening Beyond Words

The way someone speaks, their facial expressions, or their posture can offer clues about their experience. Your friend might insist they're fine, despite sounding subdued. Equally, they might speak with enthusiasm about a job opportunity while appearing hesitant whenever they discuss actually pursuing it.

These observations aren't definitive evidence of what someone is feeling. But they can invite us to become more curious and ask a question we otherwise wouldn't have considered. However, it’s important to check your interpretation rather than assuming you've correctly read someone—for example:

“You say you're excited, but I noticed you hesitated a little. Are you having mixed feelings about it?”

The Real Skill Isn't Always Listening at the Highest Level

The real skill is recognising what a conversation requires and adapting accordingly:

  • Sometimes, we need to exchange information (listening to know).
  • Sometimes, your friend simply wants to feel understood (listening to empathise).
  • Sometimes, we listen to change the way we think (listening to learn).
  • And occasionally, we have the opportunity to discover something together that neither of us had considered before (listening to discover).

When we're unaware of the different ways we can listen, we risk listening without intention—failing to deliver on what the conversation is calling for.

Listening Well Doesn't Necessarily Mean Asking More Questions

Listening well could mean allowing a moment of silence, reflecting back what you've heard, or checking whether you've understood someone correctly. Rather than immediately asking another question, we might instead say:

"It sounds like that's been really difficult for you."

Sometimes, the most valuable thing we can contribute to a conversation isn't another thought of our own, but evidence that we've understood someone else's.

Equally, Being a Good Listener Doesn't Mean Speaking Less

Being a good listener means making your contributions more informed by what you've heard.

The problem isn't contributing—it's being so preoccupied with what we want to contribute that we fail to properly consider what the other person is saying.

How the Best Conversations Are Made

Great conversations are something we create by becoming more intentional about how we listen.

Listening and speaking aren’t opposing activities where one person is talking and the other is listening. Instead, it’s a form of collaborative thinking where:

  1. One person introduces an idea.
  2. The other listens, considers it, and offers a perspective shaped by what the first person has said.
  3. The first person then revises or develops their thinking.
  4. Together, they arrive somewhere neither would have reached independently.

The best listeners aren't the people who have the best thoughts to respond with. They're the people who make it possible for the conversation to lead somewhere where the two people speaking hadn't yet realised themselves.

For Your Next Conversation

The next time you speak with someone, don’t just ask yourself what you should say.

Ask yourself what the conversation needs—and where it might lead if you listened differently.

item.title: Women and ADHD: Has Your Diagnosis Been Missed?
item.description:
ADHD

Women and ADHD: Has Your Diagnosis Been Missed?

A missed ADHD diagnosis is a lost opportunity—for healing.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Men and women with ADHD may have different symptoms, challenges, and stigmas, which can lead to misdiagnosis.
  • ADHD and eating disorders often are found together.
  • In women, the patterns of ADHD change throughout the stages of life.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) doesn’t play favorites. It affects people of all genders—and not always in the same way.

Source: Courtesy of Harmony

As I explain in the new edition of my book Finally Focused (Harmony 2026), for decades, ADHD was thought to be primarily a ‘‘boy’s disorder,’’ because the hyperactive, impulsive type was easiest to spot in school-age boys. But as we now understand, the presentation of ADHD varies across genders—especially in adults. Men and women often experience different symptom patterns, different emotional challenges, and different social stigmas. For women, these differences can lead to misdiagnosis (or no diagnosis at all) until adulthood, when the consequences of untreated ADHD finally demand attention.

Statistics help tell the story. In childhood, boys are diagnosed with ADHD four times more frequently than girls. In adulthood, women are typically diagnosed four years later than men.

Women and ADHD: Same Disorder, Different Symptoms

For many women, ADHD is less about bouncing off the walls and more about internal chaos: feeling disorganized, distracted, and emotionally overwhelmed.

The so-called inattentive type of ADHD—characterized by forgetfulness, poor follow-through, difficulty focusing, and frequent mental drift—is more common in women, especially those diagnosed later in life.

Because they often appear less disruptive than their male counterparts, girls with ADHD may fly under the radar. They’re seen as dreamy, sensitive, anxious, or just “not trying hard enough.’’ These early patterns persist into adulthood, where women juggle the multiple demands of career, relationships, parenting, and household management—while battling self-doubt and mental exhaustion.

Adult women with ADHD often suffer from chronic feelings of inadequacy. They may work overtime to compensate for their symptoms, a phenomenon sometimes called ‘‘overefforting,” which consists of overpreparation and perfectionism. This can lead to burnout, anxiety, depression, or an eating disorder, conditions that are frequently diagnosed instead of the underlying ADHD.

And then there are the hormonal factors. ADHD symptoms can fluctuate across the menstrual cycle, and often worsen during pregnancy, the postpartum period, and perimenopause. Estrogen enhances dopamine transmission—a key neurotransmitter in ADHD—so when estrogen levels drop, ADHD symptoms may intensify. In fact, perimenopause is often the period when ADHD is unmasked in women. This biological reality is rarely discussed in conventional ADHD treatment, leaving many women confused and unsupported.

Bottom line: Girls and women with ADHD don’t have less impairment than boys and men. They have less visible impairment.

Source: Robert Adrian Hillman / Shutterstock

Stages of Life, Stages of ADHD

An analysis of life stages can further clarify—for you and your health professional—what ADHD looks like in women.

Childhood: Look for inattentive symptoms, slower work, a girl who is “bright but inconsistent,” and social strain. For parents and clinicians, ask a child about the effort they need to complete tasks, an inability to keep track of time, and emotional strain.

Adolescence: Look for impaired body image, sleep loss, and functional impairment exposed by academic pressure. For clinicians, screen for self-criticism, anxiety, depression, and binge/purge behavior. (I’ll tell you more about ADHD and eating disorders in a moment.)

Young adulthood: This is a time of instability in college or at work—as well as difficulty with finances and relationships. All of this may be masked by overwork. For clinicians, ask questions about childhood onset—and treat for dietary imbalances and substance use.

Pregnancy/postpartum: During this time, a woman with ADHD may suffer from sleep disruption and role overload (having more responsibilities and demands than you have the time or energy to manage, like infant care, household responsibilities, medical appointments, etc.) The patient and professional need to plan collaboratively and monitor function, mood, and nutrition. For clinicians, never assume symptoms are “just postpartum.” Look for—and treat—ADHD.

Perimenopausal/later life: Declining estrogen may lead to worsening symptoms, particularly “executive dysfunction’’—the inability to organize, plan, prioritize, initiate, and complete goal-driven activities.

There’s another aspect of ADHD that’s more common in women than in men: eating disorders.

Source: gpointstudio / Shutterstock

ADHD and Eating Disorders

Eating disorders are approximately three times more common in women than in men. And ADHD and eating disorders are often “comorbid”—they occur together. If you have ADHD, you’re about four times more likely to have any eating disorder—and six times more likely to have bulimia nervosa.

The intersection of ADHD and eating disorders isn’t hard to understand. You may have a harder time planning meals, and chaotic meal patterns can drive binge/purge behavior. You may be more impulsive, making it harder not to binge. And food restriction and malnutrition can worsen attention, mood, and impulse control—creating a self-reinforcing loop of disordered eating.

If you have ADHD and these behaviors—seek professional help. For clinicians who treat ADHD, ask your patients about food restriction, binging and purging, and use of stimulants to control appetite. If you diagnose an eating disorder, treat it, and restore ordered nutrition—while at the same time treating ADHD.

Good Nutrition and ADHD

Nutrient insufficiency—from menstrual loss, pregnancy/postpartum depletion, restrictive diets, eating disorders, or gastrointestinal disease (like celiac, irritable bowel syndrome, or inflammatory bowel disease)—can complicate ADHD in women. Patients and professionals should be particularly attentive to:

  • Regular meals.
  • Getting enough protein (especially early in the day).
  • Making sure you get enough iron, from meat, poultry, and seafood—the nutrient is a must for dopamine, a neurotransmitter that helps regulate attention. Your doctor should also test for iron levels and supplement if necessary.
  • Likewise, the mineral zinc supports neurotransmitters; supplementing the diet with approximately 15 mg daily is wise for most people with ADHD.
  • Magnesium is an important nutrient; many people with ADHD are deficient. For ADHD patients, I typically recommend 250 mg of magnesium glycinate daily.

item.title: Sugar Could be Making You Depressed
item.description:
Ketogenic Diet

Sugar Could be Making You Depressed

Research suggests that what we eat influences our mood.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Insulin resistance, which is a problem with how the body handles blood sugar, often occurs before depression.
  • Diets high in ultraprocessed foods and sugar are linked to a higher risk of depression.
  • Cutting ultraprocessed foods has been shown to reduce depression and anxiety.
  • Stanford’s Dr. Shebani Sethi pioneered metabolic psychiatry, which treats the brain and metabolism together.
Another way to think about depression
Source: Google gemini

For decades, psychiatrists have believed that depression is caused by a deficiency of chemical messengers known as neurotransmitters. A lack of these chemicals has been touted as the cause of depression, and antidepressant medicines were believed to work by increasing them. But about one third of patients with depression don’t respond to conventional antidepressants. This suggests there’s more to this story, and new research suggests that our blood sugar may be a missing piece in the depression puzzle.

Why Your Brain Cares About Blood Sugar

Our brain makes up about 2% of our body weight, but it uses about 20% of our body’s energy. Most of that energy comes from glucose, which is the sugar found in our blood. Our bodies use insulin to move glucose from the blood into our cells. You can think of insulin as a key that unlocks cells so sugar can get in.

But when this system gets overloaded, it causes problems. When we eat food that contains a lot of carbohydrates (e.g. sugars and starches), our blood sugar can shoot up quickly and then crash. Over time, our body needs more and more insulin to get the same results. Eventually our cells can become unresponsive to insulin. This is called insulin resistance, and it can lead to type 2 diabetes.

The Link Between Insulin Resistance and Depression

It has been known for a long time that people with diabetes are twice as likely to be depressed as people without it. But which comes first – diabetes or depression?

A study of 601 adults who were not depressed was conducted over nine years. The study found that people with signs of insulin resistance were much more likely to develop depression. A rise in the ratio of triglycerides to HDL cholesterol was associated with an 89% higher rate of new depression, and a rise in fasting blood sugar was associated with a 37% higher rate. This showed that problems with blood sugar control developed before depression did.

Diet matters too. In another study involving nearly 70,000 women, those who ate diets with a high glycemic index (i.e. foods that spike blood sugar quickly) were more likely to develop depression. Women who ate more fiber, whole grains, vegetables, and fruit were less likely to become depressed.

What about the “sugar rush”? A review of 31 studies found that sugar doesn’t lift mood. Within an hour of eating it, people actually felt more tired and less alert. The sugar rush is mostly a myth. But the sugar crash is real.

Where Ultraprocessed Foods Come In

Ultraprocessed foods are products made from refined ingredients and additives. Examples include sodas, packaged snacks, sweetened cereals, fast food, and many frozen meals. These foods are often loaded with sugar and starch, which cause our blood sugar to swing high, then low.

A review involving data from nearly 10 million people found that eating more ultraprocessed food was linked to a 22% higher risk of depression and higher risks of anxiety, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease. Another study of more than 31,000 women found those who ate the most ultraprocessed food had a 50% higher risk of depression than those who ate the least ultraprocessed food.

Studies like these show there’s a connection between eating ultraprocessed food and depression, but they don’t prove that eating these foods causes depression.

Metabolic Psychiatry: Dr. Shebani Sethi’s Work at Stanford

Dr. Shebani Sethi
Source: Psychology Today

A doctor who has done amazing work in this area is Dr. Shebani Sethi. A psychiatrist and obesity medicine specialist at Stanford, Dr. Sethi coined the term “metabolic psychiatry” to describe a new field that studies and treats the connection between metabolic problems and mental illness.

Dr. Sethi’s focus is simple. She points out that the brain uses a lot of energy, and when the body’s energy system breaks down, the brain suffers. In a review, she and her colleagues described how depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and binge eating disorder all share similar problems, including poor utilization of glucose by the brain, imbalanced brain chemicals, oxidative stress, and inflammation. In another review, Dr. Sethi and Dr. Judith Ford noted that insulin resistance is a risk factor for depression.

Dr. Sethi has also written about how ultraprocessed and refined carbohydrates can trigger blood sugar and insulin spikes that cause cravings and overeating in a way that resembles drug addiction. This helps explain why it can be so hard to eat less of these foods.

Her best-known study tested a ketogenic diet (which is very low in carbohydrates) in 21 adults with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia who also had metabolic problems. These patients stayed on their medications. After four months, the number of people who met the criteria for metabolic syndrome dropped from 29% to zero. Their weight, waist size, blood sugar, and insulin resistance all improved. Also, their psychiatric symptom severity dropped by 31%.

In 2026, Dr. Sethi and her colleagues published their recommendations on using ketogenic therapy in adults with major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. Her team at Stanford is also running a larger randomized trial that includes people with major depression.

What This Research Tells Us

It would be a mistake to say that blood sugar causes all depression. It doesn’t. Depression has many causes. Most of the studies linking diet and depression don’t prove high sugar causes depression.

But the evidence is growing that insulin resistance often develops before depression, and diets that spike blood sugar are linked to a higher risk of developing depression. Also, when people with depression and metabolic problems change how they eat, their mood often improves.

The Bottom Line

Our brain doesn’t exist in a vacuum. It depends on the rest of our body for fuel, and when that fuel supply is unstable, we may experience mood changes. New research, including the pioneering work of Dr. Shebani Sethi suggests that one of the most powerful tools for improving our mood may be changing what we eat.

item.title: Self-Reflections and Constant Questioning Leads to Potential
item.description:
Education

Self-Reflections and Constant Questioning Leads to Potential

Potentiality begins with the willingness to look honestly at ourselves.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Examining our thoughts, beliefs, motivations, and actions may lead to insights and universal learning.
  • The capacity to pause and self-reflect provides time and space to consider potential consequences of actions.
  • The pursuit of insight, learning, and knowledge is not a destination but a journey.
Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

Self-reflection and constant questioning could be thought of as a circumstance that brings with it intellectual and emotional demands. At times, this may also require each of us to pause and examine not only what we think but also what we are going to do and what is already in place. This is with the added hope that this ongoing process may lead to insights and knowledge, and at the same time to always be willing to question ourselves and do the work in whatever discipline we are engaged in (Asselin & Fain, 2013; Merkebu et al., 2024).

What Is the Purpose of Self-Reflection?

However, let us ask the question: Self-reflection: What does it actually do, and what is its purpose? Broadly speaking, when we self-reflectively examine our thoughts, beliefs, motivations, and actions, this may create the potential for insights and universal learning to take place. But is that actually true?

This inquiry and question becomes particularly important in a world saturated with "all kinds" of information. Every day, individuals encounter claims, opinions, advertisements, and competing narratives that seek attention and influence. Does this really matter? Is it having an impact? Is this impact positive or negative? If it is, why is it having an impact? Who cares, and who is making the choice anyway?

In such an environment, the capacity to pause and self-reflect provides the time and space to evaluate potential actions more carefully and to also consider the consequences that may follow. As such, pause, think, and reflect before you act. What happens if we do not do this? Is that a question for you to ask and answer? Or should it be answered by others? (Phillips et al., 2016; Van Winkle, 2016).

The philosopher Immanuel Kant argued that we should strive to use our reason rather than rely on the opinions or judgments of others. But what if I have a personal truth? What about that? Who has the right to question my personal truth anyway?

Independence of thought requires more than having opinions. It requires the capacity to critically evaluate opinions and the willingness to continually question ourselves and others as often as necessary. The quest for insight, knowledge, and understanding really is an ongoing eternal process (Kant, 1784/1996).

Self-reflection that aims for insight, wisdom, and truth could also be thought of as an act of self-respect, both for ourselves and for the truth. The question that must be asked is this: What is meant by truth? Physics is true, gravity is true, biology is true, mathematics is true, merit and competence are true. These truths are immutable and nonnegotiable. Or are they? What’s the evidence?

Learning Through Ongoing Questions

This process acknowledges that the pursuit of insight, learning, and knowledge is not a destination but a journey.

Along that journey, ongoing questions provide opportunities for growth and advancement, not in the form of dramatic leaps and bounds but through what could be referred to here—at times—as comforting insights and—at other times—uncomfortable truths.

For this reason, honest self-reflection invites us to exchange ideas for the purpose of advancing insight, knowledge, and understanding. Who says so? What if I disagree, and what does it matter anyway?

After many decades and tens of thousands of hours of daily Goju Karate practice, I still occasionally encounter a movement that I have performed in the same manner for years. Then, unexpectedly and delightfully, a subtle extension reveals itself. The movement is the same, and yet something new is now present within it.

I have never waited for these moments, nor have I expected them. They have simply occurred, and now I know the reason why.

It is not because of some "mystical" Goju Karate martial arts "philosophical insight."

Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

This change has taken place as a result of many years, decades, and potentially many thousands of hours of ongoing training and practice, which has changed my brain and my body. And so, the journey continues. Will more discoveries be made? I have no idea.

However, I do hold one personal opinion: If I stop practicing, there is no potential. If I continue to train, there is potential. Where to from here? Does this question have any relevance? In fact, is there a point to any of this? If there is, what is it? Who makes the decisions?

item.title: When 'Not Happy' Starts to Feel Like 'Unhappy'
item.description:
Happiness

When 'Not Happy' Starts to Feel Like 'Unhappy'

We may be overlooking an important emotional state: being perfectly OK.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Not feeling happy doesn't necessarily mean we're unhappy. Sometimes we're just OK.
  • Most of us have plenty of days when nothing is wrong, but nothing feels especially great, either.
  • Sometimes it's the pressure to feel happier, rather than how we actually feel, that makes us feel worse.

Imagine someone asks you at the end of an ordinary Tuesday, “Are you happy?”

You think about it and decide that nothing is particularly wrong. You go through the checklist in your mind—work was fine, you answered some emails, picked up groceries, made dinner, watched television. There was no crisis, and you aren’t sad, angry, anxious, or distressed. But happy? Maybe not exactly.

That answer can feel strangely unsatisfying in a world that emphasizes the pursuit of happiness. Even an everyday saying like “happy camper” is usually assessing whether we’re just OK, not necessarily whether we’re actually happy. Instead of accepting that we’re OK, or pretty neutral, and that this neutrality may even be our baseline, we may start wondering why we aren’t happier. Somehow, a perfectly acceptable emotional state has become something we feel compelled to put under a microscope and analyze further.

The Missing Middle

We tend to talk about our emotional lives as though there are two basic categories: happy and unhappy, even though there’s an enormous amount of territory between them. We can feel neutral, OK, or simply unremarkable—neither particularly good nor particularly bad. I suspect many of us spend quite a bit of time there.

Neutrality can become more complicated when happiness is what we expect to feel. If happiness is the standard we use to judge everyday life, then “I’m not happy right now” can begin to sound an awful lot like “I’m unhappy,” even though the two don’t necessarily mean the same thing.

Think about getting a phone call with really good news—maybe you got the job you wanted. For the next few hours, you’re in a fantastic mood, and it seems to spill over into everything else. Traffic doesn’t bother you quite as much, and your friend is suddenly even funnier than usual. You might even tackle that pile of laundry with vigor and an enthusiasm it hardly deserves. Nothing about the traffic, your friend, or the laundry has actually changed. You’re just really happy. It’s a bit like having the clouds part and the sun come out, shining brilliantly.

Of course, we eventually come down from that kind of happiness. The job is still good news the next morning, but we probably aren’t admiring the laundry anymore. We settle back into whatever we were doing before, and most of the time, that means feeling considerably less than ecstatic. Nothing has gone wrong, and the unusually good mood has simply run its course.

Neutral Is an Emotional State, Too

So what do we actually know about feeling neutral? Interestingly, not as much as we know about feeling good or bad. Gasper (2023) points out that neutral affect has received far less attention, even though the research she reviews suggests it’s a common emotional state and not simply the absence of positive or negative feelings.

She also raises the possibility that neutrality may be related to inaction, which makes sense when we think about an ordinary day. Think about getting dressed in the morning or driving to work when nothing especially good or bad is happening. We may not give those moments much thought, precisely because there isn’t much to react to emotionally. We’re just going about our day, and there may be nothing particularly remarkable about feeling neutral while we do it. Getting dressed probably shouldn’t be the emotional highlight of our day.

Our expectations, however, can make that neutrality harder to leave alone. If we believe that a good life should make us happy most of the time, there’s suddenly a discrepancy between how we feel and how we think we should feel. I feel OK, but shouldn’t I feel better than OK?

From there, it’s easy to start looking for an explanation. Maybe something is missing from my relationship, or maybe I don’t like my job as much as I thought. Maybe everyone else is enjoying life more than I am. Or maybe I start wondering, What am I doing wrong? The neutrality itself hasn’t necessarily changed; what has changed is the way we’re evaluating it.

When We Start Measuring Happiness

Research on the pursuit of happiness offers an interesting clue about why that distinction might matter. Zerwas and colleagues (2024) distinguished between aspiring to happiness and being concerned about whether we are happy enough.

Simply aspiring to happiness wasn’t associated with poorer well-being. Being concerned about whether you’re happy enough was. In other words, wanting happiness and evaluating yourself based on how happy you feel may be two different things. The researchers also found that people who were more concerned about happiness tended to experience more negative feelings about their own emotions during positive events.

That makes me wonder whether some of the trouble starts not with wanting to be happy, but with keeping tabs on whether we’re happy enough. Once we start checking—Should I be happier? Why don’t I feel better than I do?—an otherwise ordinary emotional state can begin to look like evidence that something is missing.

This brings us back to the difference between “not happy” and “unhappy.” The research doesn’t directly tell us that one turns into the other, but it does give us a reason to think about what happens when we continually compare the way we feel with the way we believe we should feel.

Maybe there’s nothing particularly wrong with an ordinary Tuesday that doesn’t make us happy. Most days contain plenty of stretches that aren’t exhilarating, joyful, or even especially pleasant. We commute, wash dishes, wait in lines, put laundry away, and sit on the couch on an unremarkable Tuesday night. These aren’t empty spaces between the meaningful parts of our lives. They’re part of our lives, too.

A good life, after all, probably isn’t one that produces happiness every waking minute. Some days are exciting, some are lousy, and plenty are so uneventful that we can barely remember what we did by the time we go to bed.

Maybe that’s worth remembering the next time we catch ourselves wondering, Am I happy? Before we start taking inventory of our relationships, jobs, or lives in general, we might first consider whether anything is actually wrong. Maybe we’re just having a perfectly ordinary day.

Perhaps we’ve simply caught ourselves on a cloudy Tuesday, with a 30-percent chance of rain.

And that’s, well, OK.

item.title: Your AI Co-Founder Is Making You More Ordinary
item.description:
Creativity

Your AI Co-Founder Is Making You More Ordinary

AI helps entrepreneurs identify opportunities, but could lead them all to the same ones.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • AI helps entrepreneurs produce more, and more polished, ideas, but those ideas tend to be less novel.
  • Because AI models answer alike, founders who lean on them risk converging on the same crowded markets.
  • Domain expertise and using AI as a questioner rather than an author help preserve originality.

Picture two entrepreneurs who have never seen each other, with one based in Ho Chi Minh City and the other in Melbourne. On the same evening, each starts a chatbot and asks it for a business idea related to sustainable packaging. Just a few seconds later, they both get well-structured and confident responses. The problem is that the responses are nearly identical.

This is the paradox facing generative AI in the field of entrepreneurship: Although the tool enables each founder to work faster and with greater productivity, it may be causing founders as a group to become less unique. In entrepreneurship, being distinctive is not just an advantage; it is often the objective.

What AI does well

We should be fair to the machine. In a controlled laboratory experiment involving 124 entrepreneurs, Cristofaro and colleagues (2025) found that working with AI increased the number of opportunities participants identified and led to a deeper evaluation of those opportunities. Likewise, Terwiesch and colleagues (2026) found that, on average, ideas produced by large language models had higher purchase intent than human-generated ideas and were seven times more likely to end up in the top 10%.

In terms of volume, speed, and refinement, AI has the advantage. Yet if entrepreneurship amounted to nothing more than coming up with more plausible ideas, then the problem would be settled.

The hidden cost: novelty

The same studies tell another story: In Cristofaro's experiment, AI also decreased both the novelty of the opportunities that entrepreneurs noticed and the innovativeness of the ways they planned to take advantage of them; Terwiesch's team also found that the ideas generated by AI were less novel on an individual basis and less diverse as a group.

The situation gets worse when you look at the population as a whole. Wenger and colleagues (2026) gathered creative responses from many people and many language models. The models' answers were much more similar to each other than people's answers were to one another, even when the models were different. That is to say, switching chatbots doesn't add much originality.

If many founders use the same kind of system, they will likely be led toward similar opportunities and pitches, and ultimately end up targeting similar, crowded markets.

The tendency towards homogenization is not just a characteristic of the technology but of how people's minds interact with it.

The first factor is anchoring: When a reasonable, well-written answer appears on the screen, it serves as the basis for all subsequent developments. Instead of generating their own ideas, the founders only adjust those proposed by the AI, and this adjustment limits the range of possible answers.

The second factor is ownership. In a 2024 user study by Anderson and colleagues, they found that those who brainstormed with ChatGPT produced ideas more similar to other users' ideas and felt less responsible for what they generated. This matters for entrepreneurs because conviction is a resource, and founders must defend their idea to investors, customers, and themselves over months of setbacks. It is difficult to advocate for an idea that never quite feels like your own.

The third issue is the illusion of creative competence. Working with AI feels generative. Yet in two large, preregistered experiments with about 1,100 participants, Kumar and colleagues (2025) found that AI assistance boosted creative performance in the moment but could undermine it later when people worked unaided. The sensation of being creative and the capacity to be creative can drift apart.

The antidote: Expertise

Founders should not give up on AI use; research shows AI can be beneficial rather than flattening, but that requires two conditions. The first is expertise. In Cristofaro's experiment, entrepreneurs with prior knowledge of the sector could recover the novelty that AI tended to eliminate. Those who used both AI and their expertise achieved the most balanced outcomes in novelty, depth, and innovation. Because founders possess what the model lacks, an understanding of what is already commonplace, what difficulties customers actually experience, and where the unnoticed gaps are, they are better positioned.

The second condition is the role the tool is given. In a randomized experiment with 486 participants, Maier and colleagues (2026) compared an AI that rewrote people's ideas with one that prompted them with questions and suggestions. Both improved idea quality, but only the reflective, human-led mode preserved idea diversity and people's sense of ownership. Similarly, a field experiment by Sun and colleagues (2025) found that AI assistance boosted creativity most for employees with strong metacognitive strategies—people who actively monitor and regulate their own thinking.

The point is clear: AI works best as a thinking partner, not as a thinking substitute.

What can founders do?

  • Think first, prompt second. Write down your own ideas before opening the chatbot, so the AI responds to your thinking rather than replacing it.
  • Use AI to stress-test, not to originate. Ask it to find weaknesses, counterarguments, and risks in ideas you already have.
  • Ask for the blind spots. Prompts such as "What would most founders in this space overlook?" push the model away from the obvious.
  • Lean on what only you know. Local context, customer relationships, and hard-won industry experience are inputs no model shares with your competitors.
  • Treat obviousness as a warning sign. If an AI-generated idea feels instantly compelling, it probably feels that way to everyone else who asked.

Back to the two founders we met above: They had access to the same powerful tool and were given the same refined idea. The one more likely to succeed is the one who provided something that the model lacked: experience, context, and the judgment to recognize what the machine could not.

item.title: The Cost of the Conversation You Didn't Have
item.description:
Relationships

The Cost of the Conversation You Didn't Have

Staying silent protects us in the moment but costs us in the long run.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us learned early that expressing needs wasn't safe, and those habits still dominate.
  • Avoiding hard talks costs us intimacy and can harden into anxiety, low self-esteem, or depression.
  • Speaking up is a muscle gone unused: Start small with someone safe and build gradually.

There's a phenomenon in trees called thigmomorphogenesis: It's the physical stress of being pushed and pulled by wind and storm that signals a tree to grow a shorter, thicker trunk and a deeper, wider root system. The struggle builds its strength. Trees sheltered from the wind, by contrast, often grow tall and thin, with shallow roots, and are the first to snap when the storm finally comes.

We are not so different. When we are exposed to challenging circumstances, build the skills for having difficult conversations, and confront the discomfort of disappointing or even angering someone we love, we grow a similar kind of resilience. We build trust that we can tolerate uncertainty, honor what we feel, and come out the other side of a hard conversation intact.

The Problem

After nearly 15 years in practice, I keep seeing the same pattern show up in my office: people avoiding difficult conversations. Not sharing disappointment with a partner. Not telling a boss what they actually need. Not letting a friend know they were hurt. It makes sense. These conversations don't come with guaranteed outcomes, and there's real risk of pain in having them. Things can get awkward, conflict can flare up, and the relationship itself can rupture or even end. We're wired to want to stay connected to people, and there's something about predictability that just feels safer, even when it isn't actually serving us.

Why Do We Avoid?

There's a good reason. Many of us learned early that it was dangerous to express emotion or to say out loud what we wanted or needed. Maybe the home was volatile, and muting yourself was the only way to hold onto some stability. Maybe emotions were not discussed and were dismissed whenever they surfaced. The specifics vary, but the lesson is the same: Pushing feelings down wasn't just protective; it was necessary. It was how a child stayed safe and loved. In adulthood, these same protective mechanisms tend to persist and can quietly run the show unless we notice them and do the work to soften their grip.

The Cost of Avoidance

When we avoid difficult conversations, there's a cost. It's not only the lost opportunity to get a need met or to deepen intimacy; it's also the message we send ourselves, often reinforcing a belief that was already there: My needs don't matter enough. My feelings aren't important. This relationship can't withstand conflict. Told to ourselves enough times, these beliefs lead us to abandon ourselves, and we stop trusting that we, or the relationship, can hold the weight of honesty. And this pattern can calcify into chronic anxiety, low self-esteem, or depression. To be clear, not every feeling needs to be spoken aloud. But every feeling is worth listening to and worth the internal question of whether it's asking for action.

Change

I once worked with a patient who grew up as her family's peacemaker. Her brother lived with several mental health conditions, and his crises regularly created conflict throughout the household. She learned that if she kept her own feelings small, she wouldn't add to the weight her parents already carried. As an adult, those protective behaviors persisted. She became endlessly accommodating in her romantic relationship, overcommitted and stretched thin with friends, and silent about her own wants in a business she co-owned. The result was exhaustion and resentment.

The work started with recognizing those feelings and taking ownership of them, instead of dismissing or explaining them away. Next was identifying what she actually needed from the people in her life. Third was tending to and helping regulate the anxious, overwhelmed part of her that was terrified to bring any of this to the people who mattered most. And finally, practice. Actually having the conversations.

If you're an avoider, think of it as a muscle that's gone unused. It just needs experience, gradually. Start small: Voice a minor want or need to someone safe. Or bring a difficult conversation into the room with a therapist you trust, someone who can help you process it afterward. The more you practice, the more the skill builds, and the more possible it becomes to have a deeper relationship with the people around you, and with yourself. Like the trees that grow stronger to withstand the wind, when we humans can stay with the discomfort long enough, we build the tenacity and capability to move through the world from a place of strength.
