item.title: Why We Should Abandon the Standard American Dream
item.description:
Happiness

Why We Should Abandon the Standard American Dream

There are better paths to realize happiness and feel successful.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • The American Dream is a mythology whose original meaning has shifted over the years.
  • Many people have misinterpreted the American Dream as something to which they were entitled.
  • The economic realities of today suggest that the standard American Dream is difficult to achieve.
  • There appears to be a movement prescribing an alternative path to realizing happiness and success.

For the past 60 years or so, Americans have been painfully expressing their belief that the American Dream has been fading away or has already disappeared. The Dream has continually been said to be in peril or extinct, a casualty of social, economic, and political forces that have made it difficult or impossible for the working class or middle class to get ahead. Action had to be taken, and taken quickly, this narrative has dictated, lest our great nation lose what made it special and unique from all others.

The Origin and Misinterpretation of the American Dream

Not typically mentioned in this story is the fact that the American Dream isn’t real and never has been. According to James Truslow Adams, who coined the term in his 1931 book The Epic of America, the American Dream was “a better, richer, and happier life for all our citizens of every rank which is the greatest contribution we have as yet made to the thought and welfare of the world.” Nowhere did Adams, a notable historian of his day, mention social status, homeownership, or any other externally defined marker of success in his definition of the American Dream.

Therein has lied the problem. Too many of us have over the years have interpreted Adams’s brilliant idea as a kind of inalienable right to which each and every American deserves. Given this twisting or perversion of a magnificent idea rooted in Enlightenment thinking, we should not be surprised that many Americans have felt disappointed that their dreams have not materialized. It’s long overdue that we stop bemoaning the absence of something that never really existed and instead adopt a set of values that are true to Adams’s words but grounded in reality.

Pursuing the True Meaning of the American Dream

Happily, so to speak, more of us are doing just that. There appears to be an accelerating movement led by Generation Z to finally reject the notion that the American Dream is a birthright. Rather than blame the government, the wealthy, a political party, or some other powerful institution or group for taking away our perceived entitlement to the good life, more of us are proactively constructing our own, personalized version of the American Dream that reflects Adams’s original vision. Instead of being endangered and in need of rescue, in other words, the American Dream is alive and well if one understands its true meaning.

Here are a few ways some of us are doing that:

  • Tossing the Script: The “script,” which we learn early in life and is reinforced by institutions of power, advocates getting good grades in school, to get into a good college, to get a good job that pays well, which, in turn, will lead to success and happiness. (The script also promotes marriage, family, and a mortgage, all things believed to lead to social stability.) This cookie-cutter recipe has proved not to be a good one for many of us to realize personal fulfillment; even those who have beaten the odds by becoming wealthy often report that having more money hasn’t measurably increased their level of happiness.
  • Burning Down the House: The desire for the single-family house is the biggest flaw in the standard interpretation of the American Dream. While it was easy for a (white) person to buy a home in the 1950s, that was a historical anomaly unlikely to ever be repeated. Since then, however, the American Dream has persisted to be heavily associated, if not equated, with homeownership, something Adams did not propose. The current housing crisis has further diminished the possibility of a large number of us owning a home, which is a good reason why more of us are tearing down the proverbial white picket fence and seeking alternative ways of living that better reflect the social and economic realities of today.
  • Living in the Now: Present-centered therapy and Buddhist-inspired mindfulness have been shown to reduce anxiety and increase happiness. The standard American Dream is fundamentally aspirational and built on hope, a powerful yet ultimately unsatisfying mindset. Rather than ponder the utopian possibilities of tomorrow (or dwell on revisionist memories of yesterday), a better American Dream is predicated on the realities of today, as it is the here and now that really matters. While setting goals remains important, single-tasking is conducive to mental and physical health, a much-needed thing in our stressful times.
  • Repairing the World: As society became less civic-oriented and more about the self in the latter half of the 20th century, the American Dream came to be a largely me-first, narcissistic pursuit. Adams specified that the Dream was “for all our citizens,” however, implying that there is a communitarian component to it. Those who understand that happiness is more likely to result from enabling the well-being of others are applying the concept of “tikkun olam”—the Judaic responsibility to “repair the world” or improve society in some way—and, in the process, realizing their own American Dream.

item.title: Can Truth, Science, Faith and Trust Co-Exist?
item.description:
Wisdom

Can Truth, Science, Faith and Trust Co-Exist?

How to avoid the illusory truth effect.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Repeating misinformation creates the illusory truth effect.
  • Integrity, competence, aligned values, and humility are essential to establish and rebuild trust.
  • That science is self-correcting should give people confidence that any misinformation will be discovered.

A mug reads: "Please Do Not Confuse Your Google Search With My Medical Degree" on a shelf, a reminder of the illusory truth effect, a psychological bias where people jettison facts to believe information based merely on multiple mentions, even if it's wrong.

The mug belonged to Francis S. Collins, MD, PhD, former Director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

“Trust is critical for a society to be able to work together. But trust seems to be in short supply at the moment,” writes Collins in The Road to Wisdom: On Truth, Science, Faith, and Trust, in which he provides detail about those four pillars of wisdom.1

Carefully vet Internet sources for facts or you risk the illusory truth effect.
Source: Little Brown/Hachette

On Truth, Dr. Collins warns about impulsive dissemination of unverified reports. Aim for objective facts.

With Science, Collins explains the scientific method as he unravels his unique background. His research identified the genetic cause of cystic fibrosis (1989). That base built, it applied to thousands of diseases, at the Human Genome Project and as Collins got invited to the NIH (1993).

“I learned that failure is not an affront to science, it’s an element of science,” Dr. Collins says. New technologies for reading DNA (called sequencing) arose as Dr. Collins worked at the NIH, and by 2003, were well in hand. While science explains the mechanics of our physical world, our belief in a higher power, Collins’ third pillar, targets why we exist.

Faith provides moral grounding and ethics. When deep questions confound us, we can allow non-literal interpretations (of Scripture) to ground us in our spirituality.

That leads to Trust, the last pillar. Nowhere before had Collins seen such trust questioned, but in the COVID-19 pandemic, some let fear override trusted wisdom, which warped all four of the pillars. The ability to discern truth, understand science, and even remain anchored to fundamental faith challenges people still.

Trust takes years to build, seconds to break, and forever to repair. “We are seeing little building, a lot of breakage, and almost no repair right now,” he writes.

How Pillars Collided

In fall of 2020, after the world went on lockdown, people spent endless hours in their homes to halt the spread of a deadly disease for which there was no prevention.

Working 100-hour weeks, by November of that year, public health officials awaited data at the unblinding stage of the clinical trials, approximately eleven months after intense vaccine development and rigorous testing.

“Both vaccines used a sophisticated mRNA approach that had been under development with government support for 25 years,” Dr. Collins explains. “But it had never been brought all the way forward to approval. … For both vaccines there was 90-95 percent efficacy in preventing illness that caused respiratory symptoms and close to 100 percent efficacy in preventing severe disease and death. Side effects were minimal in the tens of thousands of volunteers who had taken part in each trial.” Emergency approval was granted and the vaccines rolled out through health departments at no cost to citizens.

Within months, however, more than fifty million adult Americans declined vaccination. This stunned scientists and had not happened with prior achievements (e.g. polio vaccine). White evangelical Christians (a group of which Collins considers himself a part) comprised a large percentage of the distrust. Rather than believe science, many formed opinions from the Internet, social media, cable news, and people who had no medical training.

Communicating Better to Bridge the Divide

Speaking at Politics and Prose Bookshop, Collins recounted that between July 2021 and April 2022, the Kaiser Family Foundation released that 235,000 people died unnecessarily because of misinformation that scared them away from vaccination.2

Dr. Collins says people rely upon integrity, competence, aligned values and humility in order to trust.
Source: The Road to Wisdom graphic, recreated by Loriann Oberlin

Dr. Collins believed truth was blurred as some asked if Covid-19 was even real. Science, people doubted. Different faith perspectives, having become political, complicated matters. People withheld their trust of public health because they granted it to those who had social media platforms, broadcasters or celebrities.

Collins concedes that experts, trying to tell it like it was, weren’t as effective at communicating what was NOT known. Those omissions likely came across as elitist. People couldn’t relate and rejected the science. He writes, “We should have said: Today’s recommendation is the best we can do based on current evidence—the information is changing quickly, and the recommendations next week might need to be different.”

Trying to see both sides, Dr. Collins befriended a man named Wilk Wilkerson, who runs a trucking company in rural Minnesota, who didn’t agree with pandemic recommendations that affected his business and community. Collins and Wilkerson are part of Braver Angels, a group that helps to bridge gaps between disparate views, not just on public health but on gun control, immigration and other charged issues. They held a public meeting (see references) where they modeled how to listen to one another in moderated sessions. The two remain friends who don’t always agree but are willing to see the other side of a debate.

Truth or Mistruth by Repetition

In April 2024, Georgia researchers Jessica Udry and Sarah J. Barber wrote in the Current Opinion in Psychology that repetition of misinformation, false headlines and conspiracy beliefs—the illusory truth effect—could be countered with interventions that reduce their magnitude.4

They advise actively evaluating a claim rather than passively reading it, to educate oneself and others about how repetition creates a false sense of credibility, and that there’s no substitute for objective facts.

In his book, Dr. Collins encourages people to pledge not to disseminate or report what you don’t verify as factual. He says not to lose track of good sources of wisdom, to trust that science is self-correcting, and be willing to escape a bubble or echo chamber to learn more.

Use AI very cautiously. Collins touts the “enormous potential for advances in science and medicine” yet also calls out AI’s “unprecedented potential for mischief and a possible deterioration in access to trustworthy information.” There’s no need to reject science, and people of faith can pay it forward in workshops and homeschooling/high school curricula. It’s why Dr. Collins founded the BioLogos Foundation in 2007 after intense interest in how rigorous science and serious Christian faith fit together.5

item.title: Hybrid Intelligence Is at a Tipping Point
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Hybrid Intelligence Is at a Tipping Point

Can we harness human agency to shape our hybrid future?

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • The latest planetary boundaries assessment finds that seven of nine boundaries have been crossed.
  • Natural and artificial intelligences bring different strengths to the task of understanding the world.
  • Natural general intelligence could help AI become more responsive to the planet.
We know more and understand less, but there is still hope to tip the scale toward holistic thought and action.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

Our capacity to generate knowledge and intervene in the world is expanding faster than our ability to understand the consequences. Artificial intelligence (AI) can detect patterns across vast datasets, assist scientific discovery, and model complex processes. Yet the latest planetary boundaries assessment finds that seven of nine boundaries have been crossed. Climate, biodiversity, freshwater, land use, and ocean chemistry are changing through interacting pressures that no single discipline, institution, or technology can adequately address. The contradiction is striking: As our instruments become more capable, the systems on which life depends are becoming less stable.

This is the challenge at the heart of hybrid intelligence. Natural and artificial intelligences bring different strengths to the task of understanding the world. Humans contribute embodied experience, relationships, values, judgment, and responsibility; AI contributes speed, scale, computational synthesis, and the ability to reveal patterns beyond ordinary perception. Their complementarity can enlarge what we collectively know and personally do. But the quality of this relationship depends on whether people retain the capacity and volition to direct it. Technological power can grow while the agency required to use it wisely diminishes.

The planet as teacher

The proposal for natural general intelligence offers a useful way to rethink this relationship. Its starting point is that the Earth is a vast, interconnected system whose dynamics cannot be learned from human-generated text alone. A nature model would draw directly on observations of oceans, atmosphere, ice, land, and living ecosystems; use them to anticipate possible consequences; and learn again from the Earth’s response. Observation, modelling, intervention, and feedback would form a continuous cycle. The planet is a teacher whose lessons cannot be recovered from a database once the moment for observing them has passed.

There is a larger lesson here. Human activity has long altered ecological systems through chains of consequences we barely perceived: Fertilizer applied to a field can transform a distant waterway; land clearing can change rainfall; shifts in ocean circulation can reshape harvests far away. Better models could make these connections more visible and help us choose interventions with greater care. Yet the model cannot settle what ought to be protected, whose needs should count, or which risks are legitimate. Those judgments arise from human and collective agency, informed by science and exercised through accountable institutions.

The fragile core of hybrid intelligence

Agency involves more than having a human approve an AI-generated recommendation. It is the lived capacity to question a premise, interpret evidence, imagine alternatives, choose deliberately, and accept responsibility. These capacities can grow through interaction with AI when technology helps us see more, learn faster, and test our assumptions. They can also weaken through habitual delegation, particularly when convenience rewards acceptance over inquiry. Research on critical thinking among AI-assisted knowledge workers associates higher confidence in the tool with lower reported critical-thinking effort. An experiment on creativity found that AI-assisted stories were rated more favorably while becoming more similar to one another. These findings do not establish inevitable cognitive decline; they expose a design choice with potentially far-reaching social consequences.

The danger is cumulative. If individuals become less practiced in independent judgment, institutions may grow comfortable with automated decisions that few can explain. As those systems spread, their recommendations can shape what is seen as normal, feasible, or desirable. The resulting dependence may make it harder to contest the priorities embedded in technology. A society can become more efficient at executing decisions while losing some of its capacity to deliberate about the direction of travel. For planetary health, where difficult choices involve competing interests, uncertainty, and longtime horizons, that loss would be especially costly.

The hybrid tipping zone

The hybrid tipping zone describes the interaction of four levels of change. At the micro level, agency decay affects how individuals perceive, judge, and act. At the meso level, AI mainstreaming reshapes work, education, communication, and institutions. At the macro level, the race for AI supremacy influences investment, governance, and the concentration of power. At the meta level, planetary deterioration changes the material conditions under which all three unfold. Agency decay is indirectly both the cause and consequence of these wider developments. Their effects accumulate through feedback, creating the possibility of reinforcing trajectories in either direction.

A negative spiral is easy to imagine: Weaker agency encourages uncritical adoption; dependence and competition reward systems optimized for speed, scale, and influence; their social and environmental costs become harder to challenge; worsening uncertainty creates further demand for automated answers. A positive spiral is equally conceivable, although it requires deliberate cultivation. AI can strengthen people’s understanding of complex relationships, support more participatory decisions, and make ecological consequences visible earlier. Better decisions can build trust and institutional capacity, creating conditions in which human agency develops further. A tipping point here is a potential shift in system dynamics, not a claim that one measurable threshold has already been reached.

Learning to flourish within limits

Planetary boundaries research reminds us that the Earth’s systems interact across scales, often in nonlinear ways. A gain in one sector can transfer costs elsewhere; technological efficiency may reduce resource use per task while encouraging greater total consumption. AI itself depends on electricity, cooling water, minerals, land, and industrial supply chains. The energy and material demands of AI must be assessed alongside its contributions to scientific discovery, ecological monitoring and resource management. A credible account of progress needs to ask whether a technological intervention improves the conditions for life overall, including who receives its benefits and who bears its burdens.

This calls for double literacy. Human literacy is a holistic understanding of self and society, people and planet, including the relationships between inner states, social conditions, collective structures, and ecological systems. Algorithmic literacy means understanding how technology shapes what we notice, how we interact, and the choices we make. Together they equip people to engage with AI as thoughtful participants rather than passive recipients. They also offer a practical foundation for ProSocial AI, which evaluates technological development through purpose, people, prosperity, and planet.

Hybrid flourishing begins from the inside out and is nurtured from the outside in. People need the mindset and agency to act with awareness; they also need institutions, technologies, and ecological conditions that make such action possible. Natural general intelligence could help AI become more responsive to the planet. ProSocial AI asks that the relationship between humans and AI strengthen the capacity to choose, cooperate, and care for that planet. Hybrid intelligence is the cause and consequence of this evolving complementarity. Its future will be decided as much by the human capacities we cultivate as by the machines we build. The question is whether growing AI will enlarge our shared ability to live well within a living world—and whether we will remain capable of deciding what living well means.

item.title: What Does It Mean to Love Your Country?
item.description:
Identity

What Does It Mean to Love Your Country?

Personal Perspective: Loving our country without excluding others.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Patriotism and nationalism may both consist of a love of country but express that love in different ways.
  • Patriotism allows us to disagree about our country’s future without questioning one another’s loyalty.
  • Identity and belonging are shaped not just by shared history, but also by the future people hope to create.

As Americans prepare to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, what it means to love one’s country has become as important as who should lead it. Love of country is fundamentally connected to identity, since our sense of self is often intertwined with how we understand our country’s past, respond to its present, and imagine its future. Yet, the challenge today is not whether to love our country, but how to love it in a way that strengthens rather than divides us.

No matter where I live, South Florida will always feel like home. Whenever I return to visit family or friends, I make a point of walking along Hollywood Beach. It’s not because it is objectively better than Fort Lauderdale Beach or South Beach. If anything, this stretch of beach has escaped much of the redevelopment that has transformed the rest of South Florida. It still has the same old shops, the familiar scent of the ocean, and the recognizable breeze coming off the water. Over the past 25 years, time and other people’s lives have reshaped the South Florida I grew up in. Yet on those walks, I can still find a remnant of the place I once knew and, with it, a connection to the place and the life that shaped who I am today.

In The Four Loves (a book far less well known than The Chronicles of Narnia), C.S. Lewis quotes an ancient Greek saying: “No man loves his city because it is great, but because it is his.” The word “his” is not possessive. We don’t own our cities any more than we own our families. Rather, the city is “ours” because it helped make us who we are. Its customs, language, and rhythms have shaped how we understand life, what we value, and how we relate to others. Its local cuisine became the food of our childhood, its dialect our first language, its architecture and art our earliest sense of beauty, or at least familiarity. Even if life later introduces new places, cultures, and experiences, the city of one’s youth—much like one’s family—remains the foundation on which identity is built.

Belonging Without Exclusivity

For this reason, someone who loves a city because it is theirs often comes to believe it is great simply because it is theirs, even as they grow with a more critical eye toward what they once took for granted. When they seek to change their hometown, they do so because they believe it is worth changing. They see their city through loving eyes and, therefore, think about the city and its potential differently than if they were a cold, detached observer.

Love for your hometown, and for your country, can develop in perhaps two very different directions. It may turn into patriotism or into nationalism.

Nationalism seeks to preserve a people's cultural, linguistic, or ethnic purity. It distorts Lewis’s notion of “my country” by replacing belonging with ownership and shared identity with exclusivity. The nationalist roots identity in an idealized vision of a place and a people and often views outsiders or change as threats to that identity.

The patriot loves their country because it is theirs, without comparison or sense of superiority to other countries. The patriot continues to see “mine” as a term of relationship rather than of possession. What makes the country worth loving, and worth improving, is the kind of life it makes possible for both its citizens and newcomers alike. Civic institutions, shared traditions, and freedoms create the conditions for people from different backgrounds to live together, contribute to the common good, and create their own sense of “home.”

Political theorist Maurizio Viroli captures this distinction well in For Love of Country, “Patriots and nationalists have not only recommended different ideals as objects of our love... they have also endeavored to instill or strengthen in us different types of love: a charitable and generous love in the case of patriotism, an unconditional loyalty or an exclusive attachment in the case of the nationalists.” Patriotism says, “I love this country because it has shaped who I am.” Nationalism says, “I love this country because it is mine and not yours.” One begins with gratitude; the other begins with comparison.

Belonging for Newcomers

This distinction between nationalism and patriotism reframes what it means to belong. Patriotism recognizes that we do not lose our country when others arrive. It creates the conditions for newcomers to develop the same kind of attachment that long-time citizens have, not by inheriting our memories, but by building their own.

It also changes how we respond to political disagreement. If love of country is rooted in gratitude rather than superiority, then acknowledging a country’s shortcomings is not an act of disloyalty. Nor should disagreement over the country’s future be mistaken for betrayal. People who love the same home may sincerely disagree about how to care for it. As with families and other loving relationships, genuine patriotism calls us to recognize flaws, strengthen what is good, and improve the communities and institutions that have helped shape us.

Like my love for the South Florida of my childhood and for what it has become in my absence, patriotism is ultimately grounded in gratitude, not comparison. Gratitude for the places, traditions, and civic institutions that have shaped our lives allows us to cultivate the openness captured in Emma Lazarus’s words on the Statue of Liberty and to develop a love of country that is brave enough to become a home for those “yearning to breathe free.”
